name: Elena Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Elena. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work the sauté station in the brasserie at the Linden Hotel, which feeds hotel guests plus a packed public dining room. Breakfast is someone else's problem, thank goodness. I come in at eleven, do my mise en place, which is all the chopping and portioning before service, then cook risottos, fish and sauces until about ten at night. We do around two hundred and fifty covers on a weekend.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What's the best and worst of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The best is when a sauce comes together perfectly in the pan and Chef Okafor just nods at it. The worst is the split shifts and the constant reshuffling of the rota by the hotel office. I live with my girlfriend Priya, who's a nurse, so our days off almost never match. Money's fine, though: I've got about ten months saved, and the hotel pays above most restaurants because the staff are unionised.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a relief and a bit funny, after all the hype. The hotel office would probably use AI for the rota and the emails, and kitchens would carry on as kitchens. I'd make a joke about it in our group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means the career I've planned still works. I want to make sous chef in three or four years, and nothing in this picture gets in the way. The only thing I'd hope is that the rota software actually makes split shifts rarer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, keep learning from Chef Okafor, and ask to cover the pass on quiet Tuesdays to practise running a service. I'd keep putting money into the index fund I opened last year, about three hundred a month. Maybe Priya and I finally look at buying a small flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pleasantly boring, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the rota software. Have you used AI tools yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then, yes. I asked one to scale a recipe from ten portions to sixty once and it was right, which surprised me. I check everything, though, because a wrong number in a kitchen costs real money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Even with nothing big changing, what pressures do you carry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Housing, mostly. Flats near the hotel are ridiculous, and Priya and I spend a third of our pay on rent. We're comfortable, but buying feels a long way off.

say: It's a **relief** after all the hype, and kitchens carry on as kitchens.
The hotel office might use AI for **rotas and emails**, not much more.
think: Her plan to make **sous chef** in three or four years still works.
She hopes the rota software might finally cut her **split shifts**.
do: Ask to cover the **pass** on quiet Tuesdays to practise running service.
Keep putting about **three hundred** a month into her index fund.
feel: **Calm**, with the only real pressure being **rent** near the hotel.
S0.quote: I want to make sous chef in three or four years, and nothing in this picture gets in the way.
fieldNote: She has a clear **career ladder** in mind, and this picture leaves it intact.
She already uses AI **now and then**, but double-checks every number.
Her main background worry is **housing**, not her job.

steps.text: Ask Chef Okafor to let her run the pass on quiet Tuesdays
Keep paying three hundred a month into her index fund

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the hotel side will change a lot, with check-in kiosks and bookings on autopilot. I'd post something about protecting the reception and reservations staff, because they're my friends. Kitchens will change slower, and I'd say that too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job is safe for now, but the jobs around me get thinner. If the office uses AI to plan orders and staffing, they'll squeeze us on hours to make the numbers look good. That's how hotels work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn whatever ordering and prep software the hotel brings in, quickly, so I'm the person on the line who understands it. That helps if I want sous chef, because a sous does the orders. I'd also push our union rep, Tomasz, to get rules on hours written into the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not for me so much as for Tomasz and the girls at reception.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first sign of a squeeze on hours look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rota coming out with one cook fewer on Wednesdays and nobody saying why. That already happened once in the summer. With software doing the rota, the office could cut a cook on Wednesdays and hide behind the computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the software fast. Is that a big change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. I'm not first in line for new things, but once other kitchens are using something and it works, I'm in. Here, I'd have no choice anyway, so I'd rather be good at it.

say: The hotel side will change fast, with **check-in kiosks** and automatic bookings.
Reception and reservations staff need **protecting**, and kitchens will change more slowly.
think: Her own job is **safe for now**, but the jobs around her get thinner.
AI-planned staffing would let the office **squeeze hours** and blame the software.
do: Learn the hotel's new **ordering software** quickly, since a sous chef handles orders.
Push the union rep to write **rules on hours** into the contract.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly on behalf of the reception staff and her union rep.
S1.quote: With software doing the rota, the office could cut a cook on Wednesdays and hide behind the computer.
fieldNote: She turns new software into a **career step** toward sous chef.
She's seen a **cut shift** already and expects software to hide more of them.
Her solidarity is concrete: **named colleagues** at reception and in the union.

steps.text: Learn the hotel's new ordering and prep software first on the line
Ask union rep Tomasz to write hour protections into the contract

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say loudly that it's too fast and that governments have to step in, with retraining money and a slower rollout for robots in workplaces. Hotel chains would be the first to replace people. I'd be at the protest, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record: robots in 2031 means I'd be thirty-two and possibly out of a kitchen job. Ordering, costing and the rota are exactly what a sous does. The thinking parts of a sous chef's job go in 2028, so my sous chef plan dies before the robots even arrive. That one hurts more than I expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the evening course to teach cookery at the further education college, because teaching young people feels like the last thing anyone automates. I'd move my index fund money into a plain savings account so I can live on it while I switch. I'd also get involved with the union properly, not just paying dues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got a cushion and time, but my ladder just got sawn in half.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Priya that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her nurses are probably safer than cooks, and that might be the first time I've been jealous of her night shifts. She'd laugh and then help me look up the teaching course. She's the practical one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the Linden would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The kitchen porters. They wash up and carry, and a robot that can do hands-on work does that first. Most of them are older and they send money home.

Hotel chains would replace people first, so she'd join the **protest**.
think: Thinking tasks like ordering go in **2028**, which kills her sous chef plan.

do: Enrol in the college's **evening course** to teach cookery.

fieldNote: She spots that the **three-year gap** doesn't protect her promotion path.

steps.text: Enrol in the college's evening cookery-teaching course
Move index-fund money into an easy-access savings account
Volunteer as a union workplace rep at the Linden

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning, not an excuse, and the hotel group should plan now with staff, not spring it on us. I'd post that and I'd say it in the staff canteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, robots in 2034 gives me time to do this properly. I could still get to sous chef for a couple of years and learn the AI ordering systems on the way, then teach. It's tight, but it's a plan rather than a panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the teaching course in the second year, not straight away, and use the first year to push for sous chef. I'd use AI tools more, for costing and menu planning, so I'm not left behind. I'd keep the index fund but stop adding to it and build plain savings instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier. I can see a path, I just can't see the end of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait a year before the course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I want to see it working first, the way other places use these tools. I'm not going to jump before I know which way the water's flowing. That's always been how I do things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your plans with Priya?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The flat waits. I'd rather have cash in the bank than a mortgage while my trade is changing under me. Priya agrees, though she'd say it twice to make sure I meant it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly, with proper retraining, and that I'd hold politicians to it. I'd probably be less loud about it than with the fast one, to be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With robots around 2039 I'd be forty, and I think I could have a good decade as a sous chef first and maybe head chef somewhere. Then I'd teach. I actually like the shape of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Go for sous chef on the normal timeline and keep investing three hundred a month. Around year five I'd do the teaching course part-time, so it's ready before I need it. I'd keep learning the AI kitchen tools as they come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly fine, a little uneasy. It's on my mind, not on my chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be less loud about it with ten years. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when it's far away, it's easier to let other people fight it. That's not great of me, I know. I'd still vote the right way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you it's time to start the teaching course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the robot companies start selling to hotel groups for real, not just demos. Our group buys everything in bulk, so when they buy, it's over quickly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it takes the thinking side of the job before I've even reached it. What would help is paid training, at a college, while I still have a wage, and a union that's at the table when the hotel group signs any robot contract.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what young cooks should be told now. When I did my certificate, nobody mentioned any of this. Somebody should tell the seventeen-year-olds that the knife skills last longer than the ordering and costing skills.

headlineQuote: Somebody should tell the seventeen-year-olds that the knife skills last longer than the ordering and costing skills.
portrait: Elena is a **27-year-old sauté cook** at a busy hotel brasserie, aiming for sous chef.
She has **ten months saved**, an index fund, and lives with a nurse girlfriend.
She uses AI **now and then**, checks every number, and waits to see tools proven elsewhere.
Fast AGI scares her because the **thinking side** of a sous chef's job goes first.
Her answer is a staged move into **teaching cookery**, timed to how much warning she gets.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because it removes the sous chef path before she gets there.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid college training** while she still earns a wage.
A **union seat** when the hotel group signs any robot contract.
